The European Parliament has reached a provisional agreement for accelerated permit issuance for new energy projects with a focus on wind, solar, grid upgrades, and storage, Reuters has reported, citing the EU Council.

Under the terms of the agreement with the EP, member states of the European Union would be able to fast-track new wind and solar developments by categorizing them as being in the overriding public interest.

This is the latest step in the EU’s push to further boost the share of alternative energy sources in its mix and reduce dependence on oil and gas imports, which this year have added billions to the EU’s energy bill.

In the second quarter of 2026 alone, right after the closed Strait of Hormuz hiked oil prices, the EU spent an average of $30.7 billion (27.6 billion euro) per month on petroleum oil imports, up from $19.7 billion (17.7 billion euro) in the same period in 2025.

Since import volumes barely changed, rising by just 1.2%, Euronews Business estimates that the EU paid $11 billion (€9.9 billion) more per month for oil imports in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the monthly average for 2025.

The exorbitant energy import bill is evidence that the EU leadership’s efforts to wean the bloc off hydrocarbons will take a lot more time than hoped for, despite all the regulatory changes and financial support that is being directed towards wind and solar, batteries, and related project.

Some of the stumbling blocks include negative electricity prices resulting from excess wind and solar generation, which have become more frequent as capacity grows; lower profitability as a result of these price developments; and still high battery storage prices. Separately, grid upgrades are going to cost a pretty penny, with investments for the period until 2030 alone seen at 584 billion euro by the European Commission.
